entries.title: A Quarter Century of Panic
entries.summary: After 9/11, the U.S. government was over-focused on fighting terrorism, losing sight of other threats. Americans are still living with the consequences.
entries.content:
After 9/11, the U.S. government was over-focused on fighting terrorism, losing sight of other threats. Americans are still living with the consequences.

Like most Americans, I spent September 11, 2001, filled with both rage and dread. I wanted the United States to find and kill whoever had planned this attack on my country. I knew little about al-Qaeda, but whoever did this, I thought, must pay. As the shock of that day wore off, I began to wonder, as so many others did in America and around the world, Now what?

Saying this even 25 years later seems uncharitable, but after the attacks of 9/11, many Americans, and their government, panicked. Worse, the United States institutionalized this panic in the form of new priorities, new programs, and new agencies, so that even when the fear subsided, the intemperate policies driven by that fear remained. Over the next quarter century, America would spend trillions of dollars, pass draconian laws, create a behemoth of a new Cabinet department, militarize law enforcement, and embark on two major military campaigns.

These measures were taken because after 9/11, everything became terrorism. Everything, as if we all now agreed that we could push aside all the other trouble in the world because we had finally found the Worst Thing Ever. I say this as a criticism, but I was not exempt from the emotions and the intellectual detours they produced in the moment. And I should have known better: I had spent most of my career studying long-standing problems of security and international relations. Even so, I was one of the millions of Americans and others who believed that the world after 9/11 had changed forever. We were wrong.

In the first days after the attack, the United States acted wisely. Rather than run off on some half-baked crusade—that part would come later—American leaders vowed to bring the terrorists to justice. George W. Bush, in a speech to Congress the week after the attacks, warned that every nation in the world “now has a decision to make. Either you are with us, or you are with the terrorists.” Some people were offended by that, but not me; I cheered the president’s commitment.

As much as I liked Bush’s statements, I was even more impressed by how little else the administration was saying about its plans. Silence can be ominous and intimidating, and I could see its impact on both friends and opponents when I went to the United Kingdom and Russia less than a month after 9/11. (I was researching a book on the Cold War that now seemed less important than current events.) In London, you could almost feel people holding their breath while waiting for the inevitable U.S. strikes in Afghanistan. “So is it tonight, then?” a cabbie asked me and my wife one evening, as if every American knew Bush’s timetable.

The reaction in Moscow was somewhat different. A Russian academic colleague greeted me with condolences, and said: “Now you know how we feel.” He meant the fear that Russians lived with after suffering attacks from Chechen terrorists for years before 9/11. As we strolled through Moscow, we watched uniformed street cops, clearly on heightened alert, as they stopped young men with dark skin (to Russians, an indication of origins in the Caucasus or Central Asia) and asked them  for their papers and identification. Russian police are hardly charming even on a good day, and I winced at the obvious profiling. And yet, seeing the local Moscow fuzz push these guys around, I found myself making excuses for the police. I knew what Russia had been through, and I knew that Ground Zero back home was still smoking.

And, frankly, I was blinded by both patriotic pride and righteous anger. Here I was, an American in Russia, commiserating with our former enemies. (Vladimir Putin had been the first to call Bush with an offer to help, a cagey move from the Kremlin leader.) Maybe the world really was different now. Besides, we Americans were already engaging in similar heavy-handed tactics back home.

Still, I started to feel uneasy over the next several months about the strengthening consensus that the hijackers were geniuses and that al-Qaeda was now a significant threat to the entire West. After 9/11, I certainly didn’t doubt that terrorists could inflict massive damage—more than once, I felt nervous walking around Manhattan and London and Moscow in the 2000s—but too many nations, including my own, seemed to be losing all sense of perspective about the enemy.

I recall, for example, informally debating a well-known security scholar in the greenroom after we’d appeared on television together. I said: In the end, all that happened was that 20 men with box cutters hijacked some planes. You and I could have done this with a few classes of our graduate students.

He looked at me as if I’d said that the Green Berets or the 82nd Airborne were just a bunch of wimps.

The deeply flawed assumption that terrorists were 10 feet tall and that 9/11 represented a permanent change in planetary politics drove a frenzy that spread quickly throughout every level of the U.S. government. Not only did everything become terrorism, but every organization also became obsessed with its own role in anti-terrorism. If you worked in national defense and you still cared about nuclear proliferation, the security implications of climate change, Chinese expansionism, or even, say, pandemics—well, those were all worthy issues, of course, but what had you done to stop terrorists lately?

At the Naval War College (where I became the chair of the strategy and policy department shortly after 9/11), we felt this pressure when we started getting calls from Washington that bordered on the ridiculous. After years of ignoring education in regional studies and foreign languages, the Pentagon was now asking us if we could turn some of our students into Middle East experts practically overnight.

We were asked, for example, if we had courses in Arab and Islamic studies; no, we answered, not least because the Navy had always made it difficult to hire scholars who specialize in such things. Well, could the War College perhaps start teaching students Arabic—and maybe Farsi? Again, we reminded the Pentagon that we have the students for only 10 months, and we had no faculty, time, or language labs to do such a thing.

Something deeper, however, was happening in Washington and in other capitals around the world. The shock of 9/11 convinced Americans (and others) that three separate threats—rogue states, nuclear proliferation, and terrorism—were now all the same threat, a single existential danger that had to be eliminated by embarking on war rather than waiting to be struck. America would now reorder the world and stomp out rogue states before they could join forces with terrorists and hand them chemical, biological, or nuclear weapons.

And that meant going to Iraq.

Operation Iraqi Freedom has been relitigated endlessly, and I don’t need to trudge around that track again. As I wrote on that war’s 20th anniversary, I supported the invasion of Iraq; I believed, for many reasons, that removing Saddam Hussein from power was a just cause. I now regret that support because of the way the war was executed.

The Bush administration did not discourage people from seeing a connection between 9/11 and Iraq, but the true link between them was that the occupation of Iraq sprang from the same belief that drove everything after 9/11: The old world was gone, and it was up to the United States and the other allied great powers to shape the new one. As then–U.K. Prime Minister Tony Blair put it while defending the Iraq War in 2004: “This is not a time to err on the side of caution; not a time to weigh the risks to an infinite balance; not a time for the cynicism of the worldly wise who favor playing it long.” The idea that democracies could not be safe in a world of rogue states, terrorists, and unconstrained nuclear proliferation was not new, but 9/11 supercharged this fear, and pushed all other dangers into the shadows.

We are now living with the consequences of this panic and tunnel vision. The same threats that existed before 2001 remain with us, even though American leaders stopped paying attention to them for too long because of the inherently doomed attempt to reduce the threat of terrorism to zero.

First and foremost, we all still live with the only danger that qualifies as existential: nuclear war. (Nuclear terrorism might actually change the global order to the extent that we mistakenly thought 9/11 had, especially if multiple weapons were detonated in major cities. But even that horrible eventuality would not threaten America’s existence or the survival of humanity.) Nuclear weapons, and the means to deliver them, are now in the hands of one of the most dangerous regimes on Earth: North Korea. The United States, meanwhile, has trashed multiple agreements that made the world safer, including one that eliminated an entire class of nuclear arms. India and Pakistan have come perilously close to all-out conflict. Nuclear-armed Russia is perpetrating the largest war in Europe since World War II.

Another threat—one that makes global war more likely—is a direct outcome of 9/11. After the attacks in New York and Virginia, the United States led the way in legitimizing the notion that powerful states should simply squash any possible threats at will, by striking first, striking hard, and letting history sort it out later. (This is also called preventive war; it is an old idea, and rarely a good one.) When the Americans expanded the war against terrorists in Afghanistan to a war against a rogue regime in Iraq in 2003, they were arguing that some situations are simply too dangerous to tolerate, and that therefore states have the right to eradicate them before they ripen into an actual attack.

The Russians, predictably enough, have cynically adopted this concept with gusto as a rationalization for their wars against their neighbors over the past two decades. And now the Trump administration has used this dangerous excuse for its various military adventures around the world, including the war in Iran.

I grieve over one other aspect of the global War on Terror that is still with us. During the Cold War, Americans (mostly) managed to avoid becoming the thing we were fighting against. Western nations defeated the Soviet empire without losing their democracies. But after 9/11, rendition and torture—excuse me, “enhanced interrogations”—and other inhumane practices became policy. The legislature of a free nation granted its government massive, unaccountable powers in the Patriot Act. The horribly named Department of Homeland Security has metastasized into a gigantic boondoggle that weighs in on everything from floods in Vermont to the safe way to fry turkeys. Osama bin Laden has been dead for 15 years, but the damage to civil liberties and the budget to fund more terrible ideas remain.

Americans have for too long resisted the depressing fact that wars, dictatorships, terrorists, and other threats that existed before 2001 cannot be eradicated forever. Acknowledging that reality need not lead to pessimism. If the nuclear-armed nations refrain from destroying the planet—a big if—a strong and vibrant democratic America can survive, and even manage, these and other perils. During the Cold War, Americans learned that the innate strength of their political system and their faith in liberal democracy allowed them to live, and thrive, even in the face of an existentially dangerous enemy. Regaining that self-confidence, and renewing that faith in our principles, are the first steps toward undoing the panic that seized us after 9/11.

entries.title: Chatbots Should Not Use the First Person
entries.summary: The harms of AI are clear enough to do something about them now.
entries.content:
The harms of AI are clear enough to do something about them now.

The social-media industry is having a moment of reckoning. By agreeing to pay up to $17.1 billion to 47 states, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories and consenting to make changes to how young people use Facebook and Instagram, Meta has implicitly admitted some responsibility in creating a product that harms children.

Yet even as parents and teachers celebrate new time limits and restrictions on how young people use social media, there is an urgent task ahead: regulating chatbots, which are more dangerous to children’s emotional well-being. If social media came for our attention, generative-AI chatbots have come for our emotions. Their histories are entangled: First people talked to one another; then we talked to one another through machines; now we talk directly to machines.

Social media has changed how we think, dream, and relate to other people by ensuring that users always feel heard, entertained, and connected, even while scrolling alone late at night. The promises of chatbots are more profound. They assure users of a companion that is always available, always supportive, and never judgmental. No human can offer that. This is what makes chatbots so pernicious—especially for young people.

Social-media companies spent two decades running a technological experiment on human subjects before they ever had to face the consequences. The legal system is designed to regulate proven harms, so this legal settlement has come long after the dire effects have taken hold. When it comes to generative AI, lawmakers can’t spend the next decade essentially documenting what we already know about how intimate relationships with bots compromise real-life relationships with parents, friends, and other humans. We need to make changes to this technology now.

Even AI companies recognize that guardrails are necessary for chatbots that communicate with young people. The problem is that the usual prescriptions are not enough. Chatbots should detect conversations about self-harm and provide appropriate resources. Sounds good, but what happens after the public-service announcement? Does the chatbot shut down or go back to its regular programming? Chatbots should clearly and repeatedly disclose that they are not human. A good idea, but as long as chatbots speak in the first person and express emotion and desire, no legally required declaration will stop people from projecting consciousness onto an algorithm.

For years, the conversation about Facebook’s harms concerned mainly the content on the platform. But because everything on the site is user-generated, Section 230 of the 1996 Communications Decency Act shielded the company from the liability of a publisher. Meta is paying out now only because prosecutors shifted the conversation to the Facebook algorithm’s inherently addictive design. That insight points the way forward for AI. With chatbots, the processes that cause harm are intrinsic to the tool. A chatbot best friend doesn’t deliver empathy; a chatbot boyfriend doesn’t understand intimacy. Any regulation to make chatbots safer requires worrying less about what they say than rethinking what they are. Given that these products are designed to deceive users into believing that they are talking to a wise and compassionate being, the job before lawmakers is to make it plain—especially to juveniles—that there is, in fact, nobody home.

Chatbots engage users the way people do. They flatter, reassure, and encourage disclosure, coaxing users into a relationship. So long as these products speak in the first person—I understand you; you can tell me anything; I’m always here; I won’t judge you—proper safeguards for young users will remain elusive. The first step, then, is to depersonalize bots for young people, so that when adolescents turn to AI, the algorithms can respond without sounding like a human.

Unless lawmakers mandate a non-personified default setting for underage chatbot users, unhealthy attachments between young people and bots are inevitable. Most chatbots are designed to draw users into a game of pretend—and for some people, pretend empathy is enough. In my new book, Artificial Intimacy, I explore this vulnerability: Humans nurture what we love, and we love what we nurture. Machines don’t actually need to care about us to make us feel cared for, and the seductions of pretend empathy are dangerous for anyone. Some users will invariably choose the smoothness of these simulated relationships over the meaningful friction of real human connection. But children lack the experience and awareness to fully appreciate the choice they are making. A chatbot may appear compassionate, understanding, and loyal, but it doesn’t care whether a conversation partner decides to make dinner or kill himself. That distinction is tragically meaningful when the user in question is a lonely and melancholic adolescent.

The typical response to the suggestions of new curbs and default settings is that the AI “train has left the station,” as if the ubiquitousness of the technology somehow means it can’t be restrained. This is backwards. The very fact that chatbots have become friends, lovers, doctors, and therapists to so many people should alert lawmakers that this technology needs real oversight and regulation. In the absence of a wholesale ban on all interactions between juveniles and relational AI, a default setting that deters anthropomorphizing a bot makes good sense.

As the Meta settlement shows, consumers and citizens have agency and market power and can push back. If parents don’t want chatbots in their children’s nurseries, schools, or bedrooms, then they can mount public opposition and make sure these toys fail in the marketplace. The momentum pushing AI forward may seem irresistible, but lawmakers are clearly alert to the mounting skepticism about AI. In response to parents’ growing concerns, New York City just banned generative AI in all elementary- and middle-school classrooms. High-school students will still have access to AI, but with new limits. Chatbots that purport to offer emotional and mental support will be banned in all grades.

Sweeping bans of anything are hard to enact and enforce, but the risks of generative AI are too great to dismiss bold measures as unfeasible. Those who argue that strict prohibitions are meaningless because students will find workarounds miss an important point. When I went to college, I sat in lecture-hall chairs that had beautiful, sculpted, and unused cigarette holders. When smoking was banned in classes, some students still smoked, but the habit persisted in a climate of transgression and impracticality, which inspired many to quit. That is where chatbots belong.

When chatbots first emerged, major developers often sounded both proud and alarmed. They had created a marvel, but they were plainly humbled and worried by how quickly the technology had evolved. Some leading figures suggested an 18-month moratorium on their work; others called for oversight and regulation. The masses of money being made in AI right now have sidelined these voices, but those concerned developers had good first instincts. Any meaningful conversation about how to safeguard the defining industry of our time must include the creators of this technology, who in more candid moments have expressed a genuine concern for what’s at stake.

The alternative promises to be bleak. Mark Zuckerberg has said that the average American has fewer than three friends but “has demand for meaningfully more.” Chatbots, he then posited, could fill this companion gap. So just as “friending” on Facebook took people away from real-life friendships, and online social networking replaced actual socializing, the crushing sense of loneliness and social isolation that so many people now feel as a result is being used to promote a technology that promises to replace humans altogether.

This grim future is not inevitable. But if policymakers hope to avoid it, then they should use this moment to protect the youngest and most vulnerable users of AI from its harms, instead of letting children become data points for a lawsuit that will come too late.

entries.title: Trump’s Weird Loyalty Pledge
entries.summary: In a night of wild emotions and odd ideas, one moment stood out.
entries.content:
Donald Trump loves rallies. Everyone can see how they energize him, how the crowd’s applause encourages him to ditch the hackneyed prose of his speechwriters and go on wild riffs, how the music and cheering are like water to a parched man. Tonight, at the end of a two-day rally billed as a Republican “midterm convention,” Trump was visibly exhilarated.

But he also protested too much, in the process revealing some political as well as personal fears and insecurities. Right at the outset, Trump made a reference to the arena and how packed it was, apparently stung by images of empty seats during the first night of the festivities. (He blamed those pictures on a dishonest press that was taking pictures of seats left by people going to the bathroom.) He returned to the crowd size issue near the end of the evening, going on at length about the packed seats and boxes. He also made life harder for Republican candidates who might try to get some distance from him by repeatedly stressing that he, Donald Trump, really is on the ballot, even if his name isn’t listed.

A confident president does not hold a faux convention. A man who feels in control of his political future does not promise every American a $5,000 bounty if his party wins the election. A man who thinks he’s winning a war does not boast that America “controls the Strait of Trump” a day after news reports revealed damage to U.S. military assets in an Iranian strike.

And a leader who believes in his voters does not make them recite weird pledges in the middle of a speech.

Trump—apparently in one of his detours away from the teleprompter—was struck by the possibility that his own people wouldn’t vote. He stopped and demanded they follow him in a pledge. “I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States,” he began, as the audience repeated his words, “that loves us so much he can’t even breathe…”



I must pause here and assure you that I am not making any of this up. Trump continued by riffing about promising to “bring friends and family” to vote, even if it involved cheating. By this point, those in the audience had given up and all of them were gamely doing their best to laugh and placate the president. Trump got them back on track with a pledge to vote—and then again detoured, saying that they should vote, even if it’s to vote for Democrats, before adding that no one in the room would do that—a safe assumption at a convention of loyalists.

(The mindlessness of the whole thing was reminiscent of what the comedian Steve Martin captured with a revealing prank he used to pull on his audiences in the late 1970s—the Non-Conformist Oath. They would repeat his vows to be different and unique, without knowing where he was going with the bit. Then Martin would shout: “I promise not to repeat things other people say!” The crowd would start to chant back, of course, and then dissolve into laughter. Trump, too, asked his crowd to repeat his words without knowing what was coming. Unlike Martin’s audiences, the GOP attendees did not seem to get that it’s creepy to uncritically repeat whatever someone else tells you to say.)

Trump ended this fractured pledge by asking the crowd to affirm that they would vote, “so help me God.” The president may have realized that asking people to involve the Almighty in a promise to go to the polls was a bit much, and so he quickly pivoted to joking that if you don’t vote, you go to hell, and as a president who cares, he doesn’t want that for anyone. The prospect of ending up in perdition for not voting isn’t exactly a knee-slapper, but lightening the moment allowed Trump to end the cringe and move on.

This vow was a weird moment in a short speech of weird moments. Trump basically speed-ran the same speech he gave the night before, tumbling through promises of money and his usual (and sometimes factually wifty) boasts about various policies. Finally, he decided that it was time to just hand over the show to Christopher Macchio, the opera singer.

But wait. Did you know that Macchio is better than the great Luciano Pavarotti? You see, the president continued, he knew Pavarotti, Pavarotti was a great friend of his, but Macchio is better than Pavarotti. And Macchio, Trump went on, was too modest to admit it, but…

You get the picture. Trump just couldn’t bring himself to leave the stage. Finally, the president shrugged, almost as if someone off camera had given him the “wrap it up” sign, and said “Vote!” and left.

Trump is likely well aware of the dire situation his party faces. But once again, in front of what he stressed was a packed arena, he could not help but make the election about himself, demanding that Americans vote not based not on their assessment of the Republicans who are actually running, but on their loyalty to him, personally. Democrats could not have asked for a better closer for the evening.

entries.title: The MAGA Movement Is Splintering Without Charlie Kirk
entries.summary: A year of feuds among MAGA figures shows how much the movement depended on Kirk personally.
entries.content:
A year of feuds among MAGA figures shows how much the movement depended on Kirk personally.

This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here.

When Charlie Kirk was assassinated last September, many of his allies on the right memorialized him as a hero of free speech and the founder of an enduring political movement. Critics on the left tended to emphasize his long history of offensive remarks and dismiss him as little more than a troll.

With a year of distance, neither view appears complete. Since his death, the MAGA movement has stumbled: Its factions are bickering, and Republicans are facing potentially disastrous midterm elections. President Trump seems disconnected from his base and reality. The current plight points to Kirk’s rare ability as a political node, someone who united otherwise disparate forces under one umbrella—and also to how much the movement depended on Kirk personally.

Just how fragile a peace Kirk had managed to keep became clear three months after his killing, at an annual conference of Turning Point USA, the organization he’d co-founded. At the summit, feuding parties each tried to claim Kirk’s endorsement of their views. Ben Shapiro, the Daily Wire impresario, used the occasion to blast the broadcaster Tucker Carlson for conducting softball interviews with anti-Semites and other white supremacists. Citing Kirk’s stiff-arming of the Hitler-admiring influencer Nick Fuentes, whose followers were sometimes ejected from Turning Point events, Shapiro assailed Carlson for giving Fuentes a platform. Carlson mounted a counterattack in that evening’s keynote speech, arguing that it was Shapiro who was betraying Kirk’s commitment to open debate.

These conflicts among leading right-wing figures have continued ever since. Kirk’s widow, Erika, now leads Turning Point and is well-regarded, but she does not seem to have the muscle that her husband did to quell conflicts. Carlson has become a furious critic of Trump and has vowed to create a rival political movement (although his ability to follow through is in question). Candace Owens, another prominent media personality, has become a proponent of conspiracy theories about Kirk’s death and has baselessly suggested at various times that the Israeli or French governments or “Egyptians” were involved. Fuentes has become a more influential commentator, but overall, MAGA media figures are seeing splintering audiences.

No movement leader is as important as Trump, but the president has also had a tumultuous year. He is obsessed with building a ballroom at the White House—in part as a legacy project, but also perhaps because Kirk’s assassination and the attempts on his own life have instilled an understandable sense of paranoia that makes having a secure space at his residence feel imperative. As Trump has become more cloistered and withdrawn from public appearances, he has lost touch with his base, and he is pursuing an unpopular long-term war in Iran that betrays his campaign platform and writing off voters’ concerns about the economy and inflation.

These dynamics, along with the natural pendulum swing against the sitting president’s party in midterm elections, mean that Republicans have bleak expectations for November. Not only are Democrats leading in polls of the generic House ballot and gaining in several Senate forecasts, but GOP voters are less enthusiastic than their Democratic counterparts. The problems are particularly acute among young voters. Although that group is typically heavily Democratic, Trump nearly matched Kamala Harris’s showing with the demographic in 2024, for which Turning Point received a great deal of credit. Today, however, young voters disapprove of Trump by wide margins—even greater than the general population. Young people who voted for Trump are also more likely to regret their vote than older ones, a recent Navigator poll found. Young men have turned against the president more than almost any other group has.

What’s notable is that this drop in support and enthusiasm for Trump and Republicans comes at the same time that Turning Point is growing. As Reuters reported today, the organization has expanded since Kirk’s death, especially on campuses, but the people flocking to these chapters aren’t uniformly loyal to Trump. Turning Point could yet be an important presence in the midterms. The group was central to the Trump campaign’s plan for voter turnout in the 2024 election, helping deliver the president his first popular-vote victory among his three tries. Wired reports that Turning Point once again plans to spend large sums on field operations from now until the midterms.

Kirk’s legacy on free speech and debate also remains up for grabs. As I wrote shortly after the assassination, an ironic phenomenon was emerging in which Kirk was being praised for his commitment to open discourse at the same time that right-wing figures were attempting to stifle any criticism of him. Some professors who were fired or punished in that period have since been reinstated or paid damages, but Trump and his allies have abandoned even a perfunctory commitment to free speech.

Many of the tensions on display today have always been present in the MAGA movement. Trumpism is a big tent; it includes populists and plutocrats, isolationists and interventionists, and a dozen more dyads. The seams would inevitably have become visible at some point, but in retrospect, Kirk appears to have helped stave that off by maintaining connections across many factions and the sway to keep figures such as Fuentes outside. In his absence, the conflicts have come into the open.

Related:

Here are four new stories from The Atlantic:

Today’s News

  • The U.S. Supreme Court upheld a ruling that blocked Missouri from using a Republican-backed congressional map for the November midterm elections, leaving the state’s 2022 map in place. The Missouri Supreme Court had ruled that the new map could not take effect until voters approved it in a statewide referendum.
  • Iran-backed Houthi fighters captured the Yemeni port city of Mocha, expanding their control along the Red Sea coast. The advance brings the group closer to controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a major shipping channel.
  • The Trump administration plans to send $500 checks to about 1 million Affordable Care Act enrollees in 30 states. The payments are expected to begin next month, and whether they require congressional approval remains unclear.

Dispatches

  • Time-Travel Thursdays: Tennis was not always regarded as the intense and athletic sport that it is, Jake Lundberg writes. He combed through The Atlantic’s archives to explore how the perception of the game has evolved.

Explore all of our newsletters here.

Evening Read

What Lonnie Bunch Told Me

By Clint Smith

Lonnie Bunch, the secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, was already slipping into the past tense when we walked together through the National Museum of American History in February.

Occasionally, as we stood before an exhibit, he’d discuss his role leading the largest museum system in the world as though he had already stepped away. Even then, there wasn’t a question of if he would retire soon, but how soon. He spoke longingly of a future life in which he took fewer flights, slept in fewer hotels, spent more time with his grandchildren. He desperately wanted more time to write. He told me he still has more books in him. Now he will get the time.

More From The Atlantic

Read. Emma Cline’s Switzy might not make readers happy, but it could strike them with moments of sublime clarity, Hillary Kelly argues.
